_comment: Seed for the OKL — real, dated, receipted lessons from the .NET platform (.NET 10 microservices: Aspire, RabbitMQ/Wolverine, gRPC, EF Core). the .NET platform is the origin repo of the encoding loop. Portable/world-fact lessons are org-scoped; .NET-framework-specific quirks are scoped repo:dotnet-microservices so they don't fire in a Python or geospatial repo's okl check.

change the id in the URL
access control on GET by id
triggers: Adding a GET endpoint that returns an invoice by its id
Building a multi-tenant API where each customer must see only their own projects
Reviewing a PR that adds update and delete endpoints for user documents
Writing integration tests for the orders API ahead of a security audit
Pentest report says changing the id in the URL returns another customer's order
A user could see someone else's profile by incrementing the number in the request
The handler loads the entity with FindAsync(id) and returns it straight back to whoever asked
insecure direct object reference, broken object level authorization, BOLA
tenant isolation, row-level authorization, data leaking between customer accounts
authorization bypass by guessing ids, horizontal privilege escalation
nodes.found_by: security review; original GET /orders/{id} IDOR survived the codebase lifetime
nodes.title: Missing ownership scope check is an IDOR (CWE-639) and slips through tests-by-omission
nodes.body: A resource endpoint that doesn't scope by the caller's identity leaks other users' data. Portable fix: push the ownership predicate INTO the query (read handlers) or check on the tracked entity (write handlers), return 404 not 403 (403 leaks existence). Require an integration test asserting user X cannot read user Y's resource for every scoped-entity endpoint.
nodes.symptom: an endpoint fetches an entity by id with no owner/tenant predicate
nodes.fix: add the caller's owner id to the WHERE clause; return 404 (not 403) on no match

triggers: Configuring JWT bearer authentication in ASP.NET Core against our Keycloak realm
Shortening access token lifetime to five minutes for the internal API
Reviewing the JWT bearer setup in Program.cs before the security review
Writing a test that an expired token gets rejected by the API
Tokens are still accepted several minutes after their exp claim has passed
Our test expecting a 401 for an expired token gets a 200 instead
Revoked sessions keep working for almost ten minutes even though tokens only last five
token expiry tolerance, clock drift allowance, leeway in JWT validation
TokenValidationParameters defaults, lifetime validation, access token TTL
bearer token expiration not enforced on time, grace period on exp and nbf
nodes.title: Default JWT ClockSkew (5 min) doubles the effective lifetime of short-lived tokens
nodes.body: .NET's TokenValidationParameters defaults ClockSkew to 5 minutes; on a realm with 5-minute access tokens that doubles every token's effective lifetime. Set ClockSkew = 30s explicitly. Stack-specific (.NET), scoped repo.
nodes.fix: set ClockSkew to ~30s; the 5-min default doubles short-token lifetime

triggers: Building the create-order endpoint that takes cart items and totals from the frontend
Adding a user profile update API with a request DTO
Reviewing a PR whose request model includes a Status field for order updates
Implementing checkout where the client sends product ids, quantities and prices
A customer ordered a $999 item and was only charged one cent
Someone flipped IsAdmin to true in the JSON payload and got admin access
Order status jumped from pending to shipped because the client sent it in the body
mass assignment, over-posting, parameter tampering
trusting client-side values, request body manipulation, edited the price in Burp Suite
binding request JSON straight onto the entity, untrusted input in the model
nodes.title: Server-controlled fields trusted from the client body = tampering vulnerability
nodes.body: A [FromBody] DTO carrying Price/BuyerId/Status/IsAdmin lets a client submit Price=0.01 for a $999 product. Portable rule: money, authorization identifiers, state-machine columns, and security flags are computed server-side from the authoritative source (catalog service, JWT sub, DB) — the request body is untrusted input.
nodes.fix: drop those fields from the DTO; compute them server-side from the catalog/service

triggers: Publishing an OrderPlaced event after saving the order in a Wolverine handler
Refactoring a handler to inject the event publisher through the constructor for cleaner code
Reviewing a service class outside the handlers that writes to the DbContext and sends messages
Upgrading to Wolverine 6 and checking that transactional messaging still holds
Consumers receive events for orders that were never saved because the transaction rolled back
The downstream service gets the message before the row exists in the database
Our outbox table stays empty but messages still go out immediately
transactional outbox, atomic write and publish, the dual write problem
message sent before commit, ghost events, phantom messages after a rollback
IMessageBus injection scope, enlisting outgoing messages in the database transaction
nodes.symptom: an event arrives at a consumer for an entity write that was rolled back, or appears before the row it describes is committed; the publisher was injected through the constructor rather than taken from the handler's message context
nodes.title: Constructor-injected IEventPublisher publishes inline under Wolverine 6, breaking outbox atomicity
nodes.body: Only the IMessageContext Wolverine injects as a HandleAsync parameter (or IDbContextOutbox in non-handler code) is enlisted in the outbox transaction. A constructor-injected IMessageBus/IEventPublisher publishes before commit — events dispatched for entity writes that may roll back. Stack-specific (Wolverine), scoped repo.

triggers: Writing a unit test that resolves a Wolverine message handler from the service provider
Setting up the test host for our message handlers with WebApplicationFactory
Moving handlers into a separate assembly and registering it for discovery
Reviewing a test fixture that pulls handlers out of the DI container directly
GetRequiredService throws no service registered for my handler, but it runs fine in production
No service for type 'OrderPlacedHandler' has been registered, thrown from my test setup
The handler runs when a message is sent but can't be resolved in the integration test
handler discovery vs dependency injection registration in the message bus
assembly scanning that doesn't add types to IServiceCollection
IoC container can't resolve a convention-discovered handler, MediatR-style handler lookup confusion
nodes.symptom: a test resolving a message handler from the service provider throws 'no service registered' although Wolverine discovers and runs the handler in production
nodes.found_by: OrderReadProjectionTests failed in CI after the repository-wrapper refactor
nodes.title: Wolverine handler discovery is NOT DI registration — GetRequiredService<Handler> throws unless AddScoped'd
nodes.body: opts.Discovery.IncludeAssembly builds Wolverine's internal message->handler map; Wolverine constructs handlers itself and never asks IServiceCollection. Any handler resolved by GetRequiredService<T>() in tests needs an explicit AddScoped<T>(). Stack-specific (Wolverine), scoped repo.

triggers: Adding a new consumer service that subscribes to OrderPlaced events over RabbitMQ
Deploying a fresh environment where publishers start up before consumers
Configuring exchange and queue names for a new event in the messaging setup
Reviewing a PR that hardcodes a queue name string in the listener configuration
Events published right after deploy never reached the new service but the outbox says delivered
The consumer gets nothing and the RabbitMQ admin shows an empty exchange with a typo in its name
Messages vanished during the first startup of the billing service
unroutable messages dropped by a fanout exchange with no queue bound
broker topology provisioning, declaring exchanges, queues and bindings
auto-provision race on startup, lost AMQP messages, publish before subscribe
nodes.symptom: an event published during a consumer's first boot is marked delivered in the outbox but never reaches the queue; the consumer's exchange or binding did not exist yet, or a misspelled name was auto-provisioned as an empty exchange
nodes.title: Fanout exchanges silently discard unroutable messages before a consumer's first boot
nodes.body: AutoProvision declares topology lazily per service; an event published before a consumer's queue+binding exists is dropped while the outbox marks it delivered. Each publisher must declare its own exchange AND its consumers' queues+bindings; names from shared constants, never inline literals (a typo is auto-provisioned as an empty object and the consumer starves silently). Stack-specific (RabbitMQ/Wolverine), scoped repo.

triggers: Adding Prometheus counters for dead-letter queue messages and failed jobs
Setting up Grafana alert rules on our custom application metrics
Reviewing a PR that adds a metrics class with several counters
Writing the runbook section about which metric pages on-call
The DLQ alarm never fired even though messages piled up in the dead-letter queue
Our counter has sat at zero on the dashboard since the day it was deployed
The metrics class is registered in DI but nothing ever calls it
instrumentation that is never emitted, dead counters, phantom telemetry
silent alerting gap, monitoring that looks wired up but isn't
custom meters and gauges in OpenTelemetry, a metric that is never incremented
nodes.symptom: a counter or gauge that a dashboard or runbook names as the alarm, whose value has never moved; a metrics class registered but never injected
nodes.title: A declared-but-never-incremented metric is a working-looking alarm that never fires
nodes.body: A AppMetrics class was registered but never injected; all five counters were dead while docs presented one as THE dead-letter-queue alarm. An operator wires an alert to it and it never fires — worse than no counter. Portable: every counter needs at least one increment call site, every metrics holder must be injected somewhere.

triggers: Creating a repository interface for the new storage class in case we swap databases later
Refactoring the payment client into a port and adapter for hexagonal architecture
Reviewing a PR that adds an IEmailSender interface with a single SMTP implementation
Adding a factory that picks the notification provider based on configuration
Every class here has an interface with exactly one implementation and none of them are mocked
Go to definition always lands on an interface and I have to hop again to the only implementation
This factory returns the same class no matter what input it gets
YAGNI abstraction, premature abstraction, one interface per class
ports and adapters, clean architecture boilerplate, abstracting for a future swap
header interfaces, speculative generality, over-engineering with dependency injection
nodes.symptom: an interface with one implementation that no test substitutes and no roadmap item will; a factory that returns the same class for every input
nodes.title: Interfaces earn their keep through consumer substitution, not 'future swap'
nodes.body: A port/adapter interface is justified only if (a) a test substitutes it today, (b) 2+ concrete impls are registered today, or (c) a second impl is on a concrete near-term roadmap. Otherwise it's speculative coupling — delete it, take the concrete class. A factory returning one impl for every input is the same coupling. Portable design rule.

triggers: Writing a review agent prompt that enforces our architecture rules on pull requests
Documenting our code quality gates and enforcement tiers in the contributing guide

The pre-commit hook described in the README isn't actually installed for anyone
paper rules, documentation-only enforcement, shelfware quality checks
a guardrail that is never invoked, dead CI gate, unused review bot
rules that live only in markdown, governance docs that nothing executes
nodes.symptom: a review agent, linter or gate described in the docs as enforcement that no hook, CI job or command ever invokes
nodes.title: A surface nobody runs is documentation, not enforcement
nodes.body: The architecture-reviewer agent was described as a live Tier-2 enforcement surface in six documents while being invoked by nothing, ever. The single most transferable lesson: a rule that is only written down drifts; wire it to something that actually runs. (Also recorded independently in the geospatial repo as error #10.)

Adding a CI check that greps the repo for names of services and classes we have removed.

dead names lingering in markdown, code comments and appsettings after a migration
deprecated identifier sweep, banned-terms lint, forbidden words check across docs and config
documentation rot after a tech swap, like the wiki still describing the old message broker
nodes.symptom: a retired identifier, service name or transport still taught as current in docs, comments or config after the code dropped it
nodes.title: Tombstone audit — group-scoped exemptions, fail on invalid regex, scan untracked
nodes.body: The compiler catches stale identifiers in code; nothing catches them in docs/comments/config. A memory-based sweep left 15+ docs teaching Azure Service Bus as current after the RabbitMQ swap. Gate: git grep every tombstoned identifier; exemptions are scoped to ONE group (a file allowlisted for a past removal is still audited against future tombstones); an invalid regex must FAIL the audit, not silently disable itself.
